blocks.text: Create new objects by copying a configured instance instead of building each one from scratch.

A **prototype** knows how to produce an independent **copy** of itself. Clients keep a registry of ready-made instances and clone the one they need, so they depend on the copy contract, not on concrete classes. The decisive question is always how deep the copy goes.

items: **Varies:** the configured template, chosen by key at runtime.
**Stays stable:** the code that asks for a new instance.
**Hard part:** deep versus shallow copies of mutable state.

blocks.text: In Java prefer a copy constructor or explicit `copy()` over `Cloneable`. The `clone()` contract is fragile and bypasses constructors.

walkthrough.note: A one-method copy contract. The generic parameter makes `copy()` return the concrete type without casts.
`copy()` goes through a private copy constructor that clones the mutable list. This is a deep copy: the new unit owns its own `abilities`.
The registry holds configured templates under a key. Nobody mutates these instances; they exist only to be copied.
Each spawn copies the template, then customizes the copy. The second unit gets an extra ability.
The template and the first copy are unchanged by the second copy's `learn`, and the copies are distinct objects. Aliasing the list would have failed this.

blocks.text: Cloning configured scenarios in a trading-system test suite.

Building a realistic `Portfolio` takes dozens of positions, limits and market data fixtures. A test base holds a few canonical portfolios and each test copies one, then nudges a position or limit. The copy is deep, so parallel tests cannot corrupt the shared template, and test setup drops from twenty lines to two.
Payoff: expensive setup is paid once, and every caller starts from an isolated, known state.

lists.title: Use when
items: Construction is costly or needs many steps, and variants differ slightly.
The set of templates is chosen or loaded at runtime.
You want isolated copies of a configured object, such as test fixtures.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Objects are cheap and immutable; just share or construct them.
The object graph has cycles or external resources that cannot be copied.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: A shallow copy aliasing a mutable list or map leaks changes between copies.
`Cloneable` skips constructors, so final fields and invariants can break.
Subclasses forgetting to override `copy()` return the parent type.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Cloning an object only to immediately overwrite every field.
Deep-copying large graphs on every request instead of sharing immutables.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records plus a `withX` method give copy-with-change for immutable values, with no cloning at all.
Serialization-based deep copy is slow and brittle; write explicit copy constructors.

rows.difference: Factory Method needs a creator hierarchy to decide which class to build. Prototype needs none: the configured instance is the template.
A concrete abstract factory can store prototypes and copy them to produce its family, avoiding a subclass per variant.
Builder starts from defaults and assembles values. Prototype starts from an already assembled instance and adjusts it; `toBuilder()` merges both.
Prototype makes independent copies. Flyweight shares one immutable instance among many users instead of copying it.
Both snapshot state. A memento exists to restore its originator later; a prototype exists to become a new, separate object.

entries.name: Object.clone / Cloneable
entries.detail: The built-in copy mechanism: a field-by-field shallow copy, widely regarded as awkward to use correctly.

entries.name: java.util.ArrayList#clone
entries.detail: Returns a shallow copy; the elements themselves are not copied.

entries.name: @Scope("prototype")
entries.detail: The container creates a fresh bean instance for each injection or lookup. The name echoes the pattern, though it constructs rather than copies.

entries.name: Message#toBuilder
entries.detail: Starts a new message from an existing one, so you change a few fields and rebuild.

options.why: The class creates independent instances of itself by copying its own state, including the mutable list.
No step-by-step assembly or validated `build()` appears; the new object starts from an existing one.
A memento stores state to restore the original later; this copy is a new, usable object.
Flyweight shares one instance. Here every call deliberately produces a separate one.

exercises.scenario: A game spawns hundreds of enemies per level. Each enemy type is loaded from data and needs a pre-configured behavior tree and an inventory that every instance must modify independently.

options.why: Configured templates are loaded at runtime and each spawn needs an independent deep copy.
Sharing works for immutable state only; each enemy has an inventory it must change on its own.
A class per enemy type would hard-code what data already describes, and no family consistency is required.
Exactly one instance per type is the opposite of what is needed: hundreds of separate ones.

exercises.prompt: Explain Prototype in your own words: why copy, and what is the main risk?

modelAnswer.text: Prototype creates new objects by copying a configured instance, which avoids repeated expensive setup and removes the need for a class per variant. The main risk is the depth of the copy: a shallow copy shares mutable state, so changes leak between copies.

keyPoints: Clients copy a configured template instead of constructing
Useful for costly setup and runtime-defined variants
Shallow copies alias mutable state and leak changes
